title: Web Design Platforms: A Practical Selection Guide
description: Choose a web design platform by testing responsive layouts, content publishing, accessibility, performance, collaboration, ownership, and migration.
author: Emily Nakamura

sections.title: Define the site and publishing needs
sections.body: List the site types and workflows the platform must support: marketing pages, product documentation, ecommerce, landing pages, localization, gated content, or frequent editorial updates. Identify who designs, writes, approves, publishes, and maintains each page. Separate launch requirements from later enhancements. A portfolio site and a large content site can need very different governance, so start with the real content model and publishing cadence rather than the most visually impressive template.

sections.title: Evaluate design control and responsive behavior
sections.body: Build a representative page using the typography, layout, forms, navigation, and reusable components the team needs. Test desktop, tablet, and narrow mobile widths, including long headings, translated text, and unusually large images. Check whether the platform supports reusable design tokens and components without forcing developers to maintain many near-duplicate templates. Preview behavior at realistic content lengths; a polished demo page can hide layout problems that appear after publication.

sections.title: Check accessibility and performance
sections.body: Test keyboard navigation, visible focus, heading order, form labels, color contrast, link purpose, alt text, and screen-reader behavior. Verify image sizing, lazy loading, font loading, caching, and how third-party scripts affect page speed. Use automated checks to find common issues, then manually test important journeys. Confirm that editors can preserve accessible content when they add media or modify page layouts; accessibility should not depend entirely on one developer fixing pages after publication.

sections.title: Review content governance and SEO controls
sections.body: Confirm that editors can manage titles, meta descriptions, canonical URLs, redirects, structured data where appropriate, sitemap inclusion, and indexability without creating inconsistent settings. Test draft previews, scheduled publishing, rollback, revision history, and approval permissions. Decide how stale pages are reviewed and who owns redirect decisions when content is removed. Verify that the platform can support the required URL structure and metadata for the actual site rather than relying on a generic SEO feature checklist.

sections.title: Assess integrations and data portability
sections.body: List required integrations such as analytics, consent management, CRM forms, search, localization, experimentation, and customer support. Test the exact events and fields that must flow between systems, including consent behavior and failed submissions. Check whether content, media, redirects, metadata, and design assets can be exported in usable formats. Document what would need to be rebuilt if the platform were replaced, and avoid custom features that depend on undocumented APIs without an owner and fallback.

sections.title: Compare collaboration and operating cost
sections.body: Evaluate roles for designers, developers, editors, agencies, and external contributors. Check seat limits, staging environments, version history, asset storage, localization, traffic or bandwidth limits, premium components, hosting, support, and transaction fees where relevant. Include implementation, migration, training, maintenance, and the time required to review changes. Confirm whether the advertised plan includes the governance and publishing features the team needs, and model expected usage rather than only the first month's cost.

sections.title: Plan migration and launch validation
sections.body: Inventory existing URLs, page templates, assets, forms, redirects, analytics events, and third-party scripts. Migrate a representative group of pages first and compare rendered content, canonical tags, metadata, structured data, mobile layouts, accessibility, and performance with the source site. Test form submissions and conversion events in staging. Keep a redirect map and rollback plan, and do not retire the old site until the business owner confirms critical journeys and search signals behave as expected.

sections.title: Run a practical selection pilot
sections.body: Give each candidate the same tasks: create a landing page, update an existing page, publish a draft through approval, fix a broken link, add an accessible image, and export content. Record completion time, usability issues, developer effort, accessibility findings, and required workarounds. Ask an editor and a developer to repeat the tasks independently. Choose the platform that supports the site's real design and governance needs with the least fragile maintenance burden, not simply the fastest initial prototype.
